cf.title: Reject wholerow references where ColumnRef is forbidden

input.subject: Reject wholerow references where ColumnRef is forbidden

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived. The only one raised, replication-ondisk-1, was refuted by the critic. The proposal fixes server crashes that message #1 reproduces, Tom Lane agreed it is a bug in message #2, and v2 moves the check into expandNSItemVars as he asked. The remaining points are code-review questions about the v14 and v15 versions.

brief.title: Reject whole-row references in defaults and partition bounds
brief.problem: Column references are forbidden in column defaults and partition bounds, but a whole-row reference such as (ROW(t.*)).f1 gets past the check. Some statements crash the server, and others are accepted and crash on a later INSERT. Andres found it while reviewing FOR PORTION OF, and the author says it goes back at least to v14.
brief.proposed_design: The patch moves the expression-kind check out of transformColumnRef into a shared helper, checkColumnRefAllowed. On master, expandNSItemVars calls the helper, so every expansion of a table's columns is checked; foo().* makes no Vars and stays allowed. On v14 and v15, the callers of expandNSItemVars call the helper instead, to keep the exported signature.
user_visible_surface: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, CREATE TABLE and ALTER COLUMN ... SET DEFAULT reject a default containing a whole-row reference such as (ROW(t.*)).f1.
CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF rejects a partition bound containing a whole-row reference.
Optional patch 0002: such references give "cannot use column reference" instead of "missing FROM-clause entry".
checkColumnRefAllowed is a new helper declared in parser/parse_expr.h.
author_claims: The listed statements crash the server or are wrongly accepted on master and back to at least v14.
The fix allows foo().* and forbids (ROW(t.*)).f1.
The v14/15 version keeps the ABI because the signature of expandNSItemVars does not change there.
Patch 0002 fixes the more basic problem, because defaults and partition bounds have no FROM clause.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane agreed it is a bug but asked for the check to move from a caller of ExpandColumnRefStar down to something like expandNSItemVars. The author posted v2 doing that, plus optional patch 0002 and back-branch versions; no reply to v2 is visible.
unclear: The material does not list which other expression kinds forbid column references, or whether each was tested through the new path.
The material does not show what error message users get with 0001 alone.
The v14/15 patches add calls in each caller of expandNSItemVars, but the material does not show how reviewers can tell no caller was missed.
The material does not say whether existing catalogs on back branches may already hold such defaults or partition bounds, or what happens to them on upgrade.

refuted.title: Defaults already stored with whole-row references would break dump and upgrade
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on v14 created a table with DEFAULT (ROW(t.*)).f1, which the server accepted. The table works as long as every INSERT supplies b. After a minor update, pg_dump output fails to restore at that CREATE TABLE, and a later pg_upgrade fails at its schema restore step.
refuted.argument: Message #1 shows that CREATE TABLE and ALTER COLUMN ... SET DEFAULT accept such a default and store it, so pg_attrdef can hold one in the field. The fix applies to v14 and later, so a patched server will reject a default it accepted before. The proposal does not say whether these stored defaults are expected to exist, or how users are told to find and drop them. Partition bounds are less of a concern, since the material shows that case crashes at CREATE time.
refuted.author_must_show: Can existing catalogs on back branches hold such defaults, and will the release notes give users a query to find and drop them before dump or pg_upgrade?

critic.reasoning: The parser expands ROW(t.*) into one Var per column, so pg_dump would emit plain column references such as ROW(a, b). transformColumnRef already rejects those in a default on unpatched servers, so the patch should add no new restore or pg_upgrade failure.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds checkColumnRefAllowed to parser/parse_expr.h and, on master, changes how expandNSItemVars is called; v14 and v15 keep its exported signature.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: Defaults and partition bounds with a whole-row reference such as (ROW(t.*)).f1 now give an error instead of a crash.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The fix removes a server crash that any user allowed to create a table can cause.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The commit messages say Backpatch-through: 14, with separate v14/15 patches that put the check in each caller of expandNSItemVars.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: On v14 and v15 the check sits in each caller of expandNSItemVars, the pattern Tom Lane called omission-prone in message #2.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: On master, expandNSItemVars runs an expression-kind check on every expansion of a table's columns; the cost is one test per expansion.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: On v14 and v15, which callers of expandNSItemVars do not call checkColumnRefAllowed, and why is each of them safe?
Which expression kinds besides column defaults and partition bounds forbid column references, and does a regression test reach each one through the new path?
With 0001 alone, what error message does CREATE TABLE p1 PARTITION OF p FOR VALUES IN ((ROW(p1.*)).f1) give?
Is patch 0002, which only changes an error message, meant to be back-patched to v14 as its commit message says?
Does the check inside expandNSItemVars on master reject any expansion of a table's columns that is legal today?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane, who knows the parser, reviewed v1 in message #2 and asked for the change that v2 makes. He has not replied to v2.
committability.liability: The committer signs for a parser check back-patched to v14, including the per-caller version on v14 and v15, where a missed caller leaves a crash open.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 four days after Tom Lane's review, with separate patches for v14 and v15.

priority.reason: Few users write such defaults, but the statements in message #1 crash the server on every branch back to v14. The patches are small, touch only the parser and regression tests, and a committer who knows the area is engaged.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review cannot confirm that the v14/15 patches cover every caller of expandNSItemVars, or that the check on master rejects no legal expansion. It also cannot confirm the critic's claim that stored defaults dump as plain column references.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: COPY WHERE clause generated/system column reference
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches make COPY FROM ... WHERE work with generated columns: they expand virtual generated columns in the WHERE clause and compute stored generated columns before the WHERE clause is checked. They also reject system columns other than tableoid in the WHERE clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut committed a smaller fix that rejects generated columns in COPY FROM WHERE with a clear error, and left tableoid for a separate thread. He then argued that support should not be added, because generated columns belong to the target table while the WHERE clause filters input data. Masahiko Sawada had shown that computing stored generated columns before the WHERE clause runs them before BEFORE INSERT triggers, so the WHERE clause changes the row the trigger sees.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This seems fundamentally wrong, because generated columns are a
property of the target table, but the COPY WHERE clause is meant to
filter the input data.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow foreign keys to reference a superset of unique columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow a foreign key constraint to reference a set of columns that is a superset of the columns of a non-deferrable unique or primary key index on the referenced table, rather than requiring an exact match. An optional USING INDEX clause after the referenced column list would name the supporting unique index where the choice would otherwise be ambiguous.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the semantics are questionable (for example CASCADE behaviour of the extra columns, nullable subset columns, MATCH PARTIAL and UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT), that the change could break existing optimizations, and that it risks conflict with the SQL standard and its information_schema. He said a patch was premature unless the SQL committee standardized the behaviour. Peter Eisentraut said that working out the full specification was the open work still required of the proposal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think the semantics are at best questionable, I think
it will break important optimizations, and I think the chances of
finding ourselves in conflict with some future SQL spec extension are
too high.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improving default column names/aliases of subscript text expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the default column name for a subscript expression with a string-literal subscript, such as data['a'] on jsonb, to the subscript value instead of the base column name. A later POC derives the name from the transformed expression and leaves room for type-specific hooks, so subscript implementations could supply their own default alias.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that changing default column names breaks existing queries, and that a GUC to switch the behavior would change query semantics. He was not convinced the new names were better, preferring names like "data_a" if anything changed. He called the transformed-expression POC a single-purpose kluge and suggested that extensible field selection would serve the author's use case better.

precedents_retrieved.title: docs about FKs referencing partitioned tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the documentation caveat that foreign keys cannot reference partitioned tables from the declarative partitioning section to the inheritance partitioning section. Since commit f56f8f8, foreign keys can reference declaratively partitioned tables, so the caveat in ddl.sgml was out of date.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Michael Paquier asked for a rewording of the new term "inheritance-partitioned" but agreed with the move, and the author posted a revised patch the same day. No message objects to the change, and the entry was withdrawn the day it was opened, possibly because the fix was handled as a v12 open item.

precedents_retrieved.title: plpgsql - possibility to get element or array type for referenced variable type
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets PL/pgSQL `%TYPE` refer to variables of composite type, including polymorphic parameters. It also adds syntax to derive the array type or the element type of a referenced variable, first as `%ARRAYTYPE`/`%ELEMENTTYPE` and later as `%TYPE[]` and `ELEMENT OF ...%TYPE`.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane proposed rejecting this PL/pgSQL-only implementation. He wanted these type operators added to the core grammar's Typename production, so PL/pgSQL would pick them up automatically. Joe Conway and Jim Nasby agreed. The author then found that a reduced patch with only the composite `%TYPE` fix gave too little benefit, and asked for it to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I played with the reduced patch, and the benefit without all other things
is negligible. It should be rejected.

precedents_retrieved.title: Bug: Reading from single byte character column type may cause out of bounds memory reads
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes text_substring() so that it never copies more bytes than the input string holds, even when the last character is wrongly encoded. This stops the out-of-bounds read seen when left() runs on a "char" value that holds the first byte of a multibyte character.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Commit ec62ce55a, from a separate thread, fixed the conversion from "char" to text in HEAD and v15, so that case can no longer be reached. Tom Lane said the patch is therefore unnecessary, and that a fix in text_substring() alone is not enough because many other text functions assume valid encoding. Noah Misch argued that text functions should be safe on invalid text carried forward by pg_upgrade, but Tom Lane said the effort and performance cost were not justified.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think we should reject Aleksander's patch, on the grounds that
it's now unnecessary --- or if you want to argue that it's still
necessary, then it's woefully inadequate, because there are surely
a bunch of other text-processing functions that will also misbehave
on wrongly-encoded data.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extensible parsing
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a parser hook that runs instead of raw_parser, so extensions can supply their own grammar alongside the core parser and fall back to it. A new single-query mode makes pg_parse_query() parse a multi-statement string one statement at a time, so each statement can use a different parser.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane and Andres Freund argued that replacing only raw parsing is of little use without hooks into parse analysis. They also argued that an extension doing anything useful would have to copy and track large parts of gram.y and src/backend/parser/. Julien Rouhaud proposed ExtensibleNode-based alternatives, got no answer, and marked the entry Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Doing anything interesting with a
hook like this will create a maintenance nightmare, because you'll have
to duplicate (and track every change in) large swaths of gram.y.

precedents_retrieved.title: Re: BUG #18741: Detaching a partition referencing a partitioned table fails with a trigger-related error
precedents_retrieved.summary: Alexander Lakhin reported that detaching a partition fails with an internal trigger error when the partition has a foreign key to a partitioned table and its new parent has no matching foreign key. Tender Wang and jian he discussed fixing this, mainly by rejecting such ATTACH PARTITION commands except where the partition references a non-partitioned table or its own parent's hierarchy.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. They contain the bug report and two design suggestions with no patch, review or decision, and they do not say why the entry was withdrawn.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P1] is about COPY FROM ... WHERE and generated columns, and its recorded reason does not apply to rejecting whole-row references in defaults and partition bounds. The only earlier discussion the thread names is Andres's report in message #1, which this patch fixes.

This is a crash fix that changes no syntax, GUC, catalog or psql behaviour, and it brings whole-row references in line with the existing rule for column references. One edge case: a default already stored through the wrongly accepted path would fail on restore after upgrade, which release notes could cover.
Apart from stored defaults, the fix is parse-time only. It has no WAL, on-disk or wire protocol change, and the v14/15 versions keep the expandNSItemVars signature.

The patch adds a parse-time check that rejects whole-row references in defaults and partition bounds, and so removes a crash that any user allowed to create a table can cause; it adds no privilege, role or exposure. Defaults and partition bounds already stored on back branches are outside the security angle and belong to the upgrade and backpatch angle.

This is a crash fix in the parser. Tom Lane, who knows the area, engaged and asked for the check to move into expandNSItemVars, and v2 does that on master. The new helper only centralizes a check that already exists, and its cost is an expression-kind test per table-column expansion, which is negligible. On v14/15 the check sits in each caller of expandNSItemVars, which is the omission-prone pattern Tom objected to in message #2. That risk is small because back branches rarely gain new callers, and whether every caller is covered is a code-review question, not a design one. [P1] is about COPY WHERE semantics and does not apply.

This is a crash fix for a parser check that misses whole-row references, and no existing feature, extension or hook can block such defaults or partition bounds. The patch extends the existing column-reference check through a shared helper, so it adds no second mechanism. P1 is about COPY WHERE semantics and does not apply.

This is a crash bug fix, so the demand case does not depend on user requests. Statements a user can type crash the server or store defaults that crash a later INSERT, and Tom Lane agreed it is a bug (message #2). Nobody uses the forbidden construct on purpose, so the patch costs users nothing. Precedent [P1] is about a feature request in COPY WHERE and does not apply.
